paras: The killing of a Black youth near Camden, Arkansas, was the shooting of a colored farmer's son by a white man and two companions, who took him out of a church service and shot him before about 125 onlookers, as reported in July 1919. The New York Age cited the case as an example of "Southern manners" and called it the "murder of an unoffending youth."
According to the New York Age, a white man and a colored farmer had a fight near Camden. The farmer was "about to kill the white man" when his son stopped him, after which the farmer fled.

The white man then enlisted "two other ruffians" and went to a church where the youth was attending a service. The three men took the youth out of the church and shot him in front of about 125 onlookers. The report gives no date, no names and no account of what the onlookers did.
No report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The only account found is an unsigned editorial titled "Southern Manners" in the New York Age of July 12, 1919, which said the incident "was reported" but did not name its source. The editorial set the Camden killing beside a sheriff-backed threat to eject three sergeants from a hotel in St. Matthews, South Carolina, and an insulting bank notice in Houston, Texas. It described the youth as one "who had restrained his father from slaying the man who became his murderer," stressing that the victim had saved his killer's life. The editorial closed with the remark that "some people contend that the White South is civilized."

bases: A1 reports that a white man and two others took a Black farmer's son out of a church and shot him in front of about 125 onlookers, with no lawful authority mentioned.

A1 says three white men (the man and 'two other ruffians') seized the youth from a church and shot him, calling it 'murder', which meets killing, illegality and group size; the only motive the text implies is retaliation for the father's fight, and the account rests on one undated, second-hand editorial summary.
The only report found is the New York Age editorial (A1), which says the incident 'was reported' without naming its source.
